segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We’re talking for a little while here. The things we’re going to talk about is for the students to hear us talking. That’s what it is for.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: In Cherokee?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: All Cherokee.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: For them to learn.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They might hear something to learn, from you two talking.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: First thing I’m going to ask you is what is your English and Cherokee names?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: As for me, Wa⁠li⁠, ᏩᎵ, is my name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: ᏩᎵ, Wa⁠li⁠.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, in Cherokee. Wallora in English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wallora. Wallora Kingfisher is your name. What about you?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Oleta Pritchett in English, in Cherokee Ga⁠li⁠lo, ᎦᎵᎶ.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: ᎦᎵᎶ, Ga⁠li⁠lo. What does that mean, ᎦᎵᎶ?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Something pretty like U⁠li⁠lo, ᎤᎵᎶ.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I thought you were gonna say ‘Crazy’.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Someone that’s got a good mind.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That’s why they didn’t name me that.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I don’t know what that means.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now, Wallora, where were you born, and, also, what year?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Man... ’30, ’37... Piney, I don’t know how to say it in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No⁠tsi, ᏃᏥ.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: No⁠tsi, ᏃᏥ. Yeah, it’s No⁠tsi, ᏃᏥ. I forgot. I mean, that’s where we lived around that time, Jay.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were you born at home, when you were born?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, oh yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s happened a lot.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Oh yeah, it’s been a long time ago.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I was born in old Eugee, but now it’s all water. That’s why they covered where I was born. What about you, Oleta?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I forgot. October 5, 1944, I was born. Bunch, Oklahoma. I was also born at home. My grandma helped my mom. They called them midwives. She was a helper, for that kind of thing, my grandmother.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess when they were around, a long time ago.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, they were around a long time ago.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now you grew up in Piney, Wallora?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, by the water. My grandpa lived by the water.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There’s still a creek there?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s my creek.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you reckon there are still crawdads living there?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I don’t know. I really want some crawdads. I was just telling her this morning, “Boy, I want some crawdads.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She’s got her eye out for them.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah. Go get them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Imma go look for some crawdads. What about you Oleta, where did you grew up at?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Just there at Bunch, South Bunch. There was a school there that went from kindergarten... no, not kindergarten—first through eighth grade. I finished there. Cave Spring. Then, later, Sequoyah

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was it like to grow up? Did you all live by yourselves, or did someone live close by?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Not really close. Not like it is now. It wasn’t like that. They lived way over there --

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: -- way over there?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: My aunt and uncle lived way over there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was the same for you, too, ain’t it [Wallora]?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, it was the same.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, it was like that, back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it still like it was, where you lived, Wallora?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: No, there’s a lot of people living there now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you two were growing up, the things the kids have nowadays to play with... What about you? What did you two find to play with, back then?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: And me, it was mud pies. That’s what I played with all the time, mud pies.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Mud pies. Yeah, really. You didn’t have dolls?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, no. Not really.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: That was later, huh?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I had a doll my mom made. That’s what I played with.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You don’t have it these days?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My wife has one that someone made 35 years ago.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I should have, and I didn’t think... That’s good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don’t know. Maybe she bought them somewhere.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. What about you?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I had one [doll] like that, too. I don’t know if Mom made it, or if someone else made it. Back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s that old?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: ’Long time ago. We’re about the same age. Yeah, that’s all they used to make. And, cans—you know, we played with. That’s what we used for cars.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There was nothing like that.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They didn’t have automobiles, then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: As I was growing up... they were looking for socks. They couldn’t find any. We made them [used them] to play ball with.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, really. They used to use those, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We were throwing socks around. Somebody would be looking for their socks. They would be flying by as they’re looking for them.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: We didn’t have any kind of toys like that, back then. We didn’t have new toys like today. And these days, they don’t appreciate it. No matter what you give them, they will play with it for a little while. It’ll just be sitting there. After a while, it’ll be tore up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When the boys were growing up, we would buy them things to play with. They would just play with it for a little while, and they would go pick something else up. Something that wasn’t worth anything.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: That’s what I was telling my kids. Everything I made myself I would play with more.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: The stuff that was bought at the store. I was saying the same thing, that’s how they were sometimes. I remember one time I was making a boat with a sail, and I put it in a pond. It would go by itself. I really felt great that I was playing with something like that.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: We appreciated stuff back then. These days, they don’t appreciate it.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Airplane paper.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, a plane.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: To fly with.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I used to like to play with that.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: It was interesting to see paper flying by itself.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How different is it, nowadays, from when you grew up?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: A lot, right? And the kids are really different. A long time ago we believed, especially me. When my mom would say it one time... When we would be sitting in church, if we were doing something and Mom would turn around, we knew. When we get home, we were gonna get a whipping.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: That’s what I mean, I believe in the switch.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: You couldn’t even go outside at church. We had to just sit there.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: That peach limb, my mom would have it leaning like this. [gestures]

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: It was like that, too.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: She would say, “I’m gonna whip you with that switch.”

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Sometimes I would pee because I was so scared. Then I would get in trouble—when I would do that—then I would get a whopping.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Nowadays the kids would say, “I’m gonna call DHS.” “Go ahead and call them. Here’s the phone.”

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: These days, kids—that’s not good, is it?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: The government has completely ruined the kids.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s right. That’s why the kids are always acting out, the kids.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: They’re still continuing that, doing that, the kids. Really.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: My dad said, “If I didn’t love you, I wouldn’t be whipping you.” Right? That what he said to me.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Don’t be loving me.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: You really love me, don’t you, right? I was really mean.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: They were really doing good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. Y’all were talking about church. There used to be deacons, back then. You would be scared.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: U⁠da⁠sa⁠di⁠, ᎤᏓᏌᏗ, would have a long stick, back then. He would go like this [gestures] and say, “Go sit by your mom.”

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And, one time, me and Mom were going to church, just when I was this [gestures] tall. She sat where the women sat, and I sat next to her. And after while the deacon he did this [gestures], “Go sit on the men’s side.”

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: For you to move.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They taught us hard, and it was good. If we would have just known that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about y’all were talking about, where y’all grew up. Do y’all ever go back and think about that—a long time ago? It was like this, back then, do you think about that?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: You can just see it, sometimes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I wished it could still be like that, nowadays. Do you two think that, sometimes?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: And where we were born, it’s all woods. White people bought it and fenced it up, all the land.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That’s what I was telling the kids—it was different back then. The kids were nice, and they would behave.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: It because they were whipping us, that’s why we knew.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: As for me, my grandma, I never got to know [her]. She went on when I was a baby. One of my mom’s aunts told me to “Call her grandma,” she told me. She had land in Bull Hollow, [Oklahoma] around more than 400 acres. She had land. There’s a creek on her land. At some point, she put an iron kettle and a tub. People would come and wash clothes. Sometimes, I would go over there, when I was little. Early in the morning you would already see smoke, someone would already be washing.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They used to heat it up, is what they would do, a long time ago.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They used to heat it up, and there would be a chair sitting there, close. There would be two tubs there, and it would be there, and they would wash in it. Sometimes, somebody would show up—they would tell them to “Go eat, we’re cooking.” Every once in a while we’d go and eat with them.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: People back then were really generous. And they also helped each other.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: At some point, [Grandma] she thought about selling. A White man showed up. “If you buy this,” she told the White man, “If you buy this, would you still keep it open, so people can continue to keep washing their clothes?” “Yeah, yeah, yeah, Mrs Soldier. I’ll have it open,” he told her. He did that for about a year. After that year ended, he fenced it. After he fenced, the water dried up. That was a good creek, back then. That’s what can happen, I think about that sometimes, God has gave us the creek and water, I think.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They’re stingy huh? Even to [allow others to] hunt crawdads.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That was a long time, and now there’s a little water running.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Then it dries up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What good things do you two remember, when you two were kids growing up? Or when y’all were getting whoppings—when they were teaching you two?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I’m glad now that they were whopping me. I wouldn’t have learned anything if they didn’t do that to me. It was good when I was going to school, I liked going to school. We were walking about three --

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: -- miles --

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: -- Yeah, miles, or more. Walking. Early in the morning, I would go to school. I would like to do that, and I would go through the woods. Me and my brother. That’s what I liked.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I remember the late Herbert. We used to go to church at Brush Creek, a long time ago, when I was growing up. Up on the hill, in the field, there was Brush Creek Church. He used to walk there. At night, after church. He used to have a road, close to where you all are from.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: He had a straight road.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: A lot of them had roads in the woods.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And, too, at night, they would be carrying --

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: -- a light.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He wasn’t the only one who had that road, I think. Someone else had that road, too.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: There was more people using cars.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now you’d be scared.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: You can’t go anywhere after dark. Those ‘Doers’ would be standing there, somewhere.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: We have bears, too, nowadays. You wouldn’t see anything like that, back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And someone would have a garden, somewhere.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Or Bigfoot.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Or Bigfoot, standing there. Yeah, that’s what they talk about, but I’ve never heard anything like that. “Oh, we seen Bigfoot,” they would say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, and one time I went to New Cloud. What was it... I was supposed to preach. It was dark when we dismissed [finished]. There was a lot of cars on the road. And, also, I don’t know what... a TV station there, too. What were they doing there, I asked. I don’t know who it was. They were looking for Bigfoot.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Really, making themselves tired.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: For no reason, they were going around.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Haw, really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you two just grew up around there, nowhere else? Y’all just ended up in Jay.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: We ended up there, for good.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: As for me, that’s where I ended up. I’ve never been anywhere else. Where I grew up is still where I’m at.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That was the only way y’all came.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: South Bunch.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When y’all were going around.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: You know where you were talking about going to school. Was it South Bunch or Kentucky [school]?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: South Bunch.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Is that where Kentucky was?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: That was the name of it, Kentucky School.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I understand now, I know where it’s at.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Kentucky School.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: They had changed it.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: No, that’s what it was always called. I don’t know why. They just called it Kentucky School.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Is it still there today, or does someone live there?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: No, I don’t think so. It burned, someone burned it. Yeah, Charlie and Doris live up the hill.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, on the hill.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: A lot of [unintelligible]... and, that was the only place for us to go to: Kentucky School. Different. They were all Indians, then. Not one White person going to school there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did y’all speak all Cherokee?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: We spoke all Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they get on to you for speaking Cherokee?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: No, not back then. It wasn’t until I got to Sequoyah (School) when I got in trouble. But we still spoke. But nowadays they say, “Who taught you and how did you learn?” We heard Mom and Dad talk it, and that’s how we learned.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: From our homes.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, from our homes.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Nowadays, they want to learn Cherokee. It’s hard to learn that way [as an additional language]. You have to grow up with it, is what I think.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: The conversation type, it’s hard. They can’t remember different things.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes, when I first started, they got on to me for struggling to talk English. It’s still that way. But around fifth and sixth grade, I was still learning a little bit.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, it was like that, we didn’t know. This one girl was funny. She wasn’t talking English, she was only talking Cherokee. She was sitting towards the front. She wasn’t talking—she looked like a White person, but not really. They asked that girl her name, and I think she said Carolyn. Then the One-that-didn’t-talk-Cherokee said, “Carolyn,” she said. “Oh you both got the same name.” She didn’t know what to say because she didn’t know what they were saying to her. What they were asking her. She just said the same thing.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I didn’t know English, really didn’t. One person said, “I’m looking for your mom. When is your mom going to be back?” they said to me in English. “I don’t know, ‘minutes’,” I told them. “Minutes,” that’s all I could say. They laughed at me the rest of the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I forgot. One time to one Cherokee girl, they were asking her questions and they wanted her to say ‘pie’ but she didn’t understand. “What does your mom cook for you on your birthday?” “Oh, pie I eat,” she said. “OK, spell,” they told her.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “Pie-I-E”

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They would just say whatever they wanted. If they would think it just made sense.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Just the way it was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time there was a Cherokee, towards-Kenwood. Where the Wolfs were a long time ago. One of the boys, the oldest, was always in jail. One time, they came to Kenwood and they caught him. “Hey where you take my boy?” they said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “Jail.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “Jail?”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They left. And there was a White guy that owned a store on this side, close to Kenwood. It was a big building. He was a Cherokee speaker—he learned to speak Cherokee right there in Kenwood. She showed up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “What do you need, Mrs. Wolf?”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “Me use phone.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “Right there it is, go use it,” he told her. “Hello jail?” she said. She was wanting to talk to her son, and she said ‘hello jail.’

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They really did just talk Cherokee back then, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Especially Kenwood. Somebody was telling me, “Kenwood, we don’t talk English there,” they told me. If we wanna charge something, we can talk it.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: The babies can talk Cherokee in Kenwood. It’s good it’s like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about, what’s their names? The Nofires. Where he’s pastoring?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Oak Ridge.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time there was little kids there, and they all were talking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They all talk, at Bell School, too—they all talk Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That amazes me. The kids from that way were running around talking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Good.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Jerry Nofire, he the pastor…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did you work around, back then? Where did you two work around, back then?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: As for me, I worked at the chicken plant for the longest time. I cleaned houses—that’s what I started out working [as], then the chicken plant.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Which one did you like?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: The chicken plant.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Some of the people talk about where they work they say tsi⁠ta⁠go, ᏥᏔᎪ.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Tsi⁠ta⁠go, ᏥᏔᎪ.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, tsi⁠ta⁠go, ᏥᏔᎪ. When they say that… What are they saying? I thought they were saying ‘Chicago’. I was thinking I didn’t understand it. Then I asked, and someone told me, “I was working at the chicken plant.” Oh, OK...

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah that what they say, tsi⁠ta⁠go, ᏥᏔᎪ, chicken plant.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Chicago.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Or, you live there.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That’s why my hands are crippled—from working there for so long.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Arthritis.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you, Oleta?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I first started, too, working at the canning factory in Stilwell. I worked there for a little while. Then I started going to school. Then they hired me at the school. I worked for Cherokee Nation for 11 years as a field specialist. I worked that long. When I finished at Northeastern, I was hired by Westville. They hired me there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about for instance, in English they say ‘hobbies’. Don’t you two have anything?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Hobbies?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Quilting is what I like—quilting.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Cooking.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Cooking?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: She a good cook, too.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I like to make pies.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Does that One-sitting-there go there?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Go eat her pies.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And me, yesterday, I was treated good for Father’s Day. They took me to eat in Springdale. As we were coming back, my wife’s phone rang. “Where were you at today?” We didn’t have church, yesterday.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: We didn’t either, we didn’t have electricity.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “We got something for you.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “What is it?”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “Just come get it.”

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I bet you went right after it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I went right after it. When we got there, it was sitting there. “What is this?” It was huckleberry pie.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Who baked it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The One-they-call-Lena.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Oh, Lena Stick. She’s a really good baker. Yeah, she was good back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “Where did she go? I wanna thank her for it.” “She already went to hunt huckleberry,” they said. She just found it, then gave [away] that pie.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: She picked it.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That’s good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah-lee.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Don’t talk about that, cause we’re hungry.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They must really care about you, when they gave you that. Nobody will give anything like that.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, really. It expensive, they’re expensive.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: They thought a lot about you.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess so. They had to, to give me a huckleberry pie.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Somebody loves me, you would be saying.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: How much do they say a gallon cost?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh man, quite a bit, $50 or $70.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, about that much. It’s high.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Are they selling it somewhere?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, some of them. It’s hard to find, they say.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Just some are looking for it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They say it’s good.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, it is. I’d like to have some.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: “The game refuge, they don’t let them,” Lena said. I don’t know where she picked it.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Because of the deer.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: “‘You’re robbing the animals,’ they told us,” Lena said. “‘The animals are robbing us,’ I told them.” That’s what they were saying.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: They are huh? We had it first.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, game warden...

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Her late brother—his name was Larry Stick, but he’s not alive now—boy, if he would go out there, after a while, he would bring back mushrooms.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, he liked to do that, that-One.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He never missed anything. He would give me a sack full of mushrooms.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: The ones that this tall [gestures].

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Nobody would do that for you, these days.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They would charge you, these days. “If you pay me this much, I’ll give it to you.”

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Just yesterday, a woman came and had some blackberries, I guess about this much bag [gestures]—$40.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Were they blueberries?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: No, they were blackberries.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Blackberries, ka⁠nu⁠ga⁠tli, ᎧᏄᎦᏟ.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ka⁠nu⁠ga⁠tli, ᎧᏄᎦᏟ.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: For $40. No, I can’t do it.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: And, also that dewberry is really good, right? When it first ripe that blackberry --

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: -- Yeah, she wanted $40 for it. She didn’t even pick it, either. I don’t think so. If you pick it, it’s worth it. But it’s hard work picking it.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: “I could eat that up, really quick,” I would have told her.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I pick it myself, as for me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But when you think about it, there would be a big snake.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Ticks, too, red ticks [chiggers, Trombiculid mites’ parasitic larvae].

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That’s why I don’t do it no more.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Those little ticks will crawl on you.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They’ll drive you crazy.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: No, I don’t do that.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Me, neither.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many siblings were there, when you were growing up?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Nine.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nine of you.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: But one passed when it was a baby. So only eight of us grew up. Four brothers, tso⁠gi⁠do, ᏦᎩᏙ. And two sisters—there was three of us, there was four of us [girls] but one died when it was a baby. Eight.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Eight of you.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, eight.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What were your parents' names?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: My mom was Iva Turner Daugherty.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Daugherty.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Charlie Daugherty.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Charlie Daugherty.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: My grandma was Diane Bird.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Diane Bird.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Especially wise.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you, Oleta, how many of y’all?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Five.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Five of y’all.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Two of us girls, and three boys.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What were your parents’ names?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Sally was the name of my mom, and Dad was Joe, Joe Adair.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Joe Adair.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: When I was baby, he died. He was in a car wreck. And... What was his name? Gonzales. Leo... no, not Leo, but Andy. Andy was with him, when he wrecked the car. My dad was the only one that was killed. And Andy was in the hospital for a long time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s probably why he became a preacher.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s probably right. Yeah, and because he was really wild.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Is he still alive?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: No, he died. He was wild.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Say, your parents, you alls’ parents, when did they meet? Did they ever tell y’all?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: As for me, Piney.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they find each other at church?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: No, but Mom grew up in Piney. And Dad, he was from Stilwell.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: The Daughertys.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, they live that way, the Daughertys. What about your grandma, and grandpa, what were their names?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: My grandpa was Wi⁠li, ᏫᎵ.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: William.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: William. What’s his last name? I don’t remember his last name... Do you know? You haven’t heard? William...

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your mom’s side, or your dad’s side?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: William Turner—that’s it. My mom’s name was Ga⁠no⁠, ᎦᏃ, in Cherokee. My dad came from Stilwell. His mom was Diane Bird. My grandma.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you, Oleta?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I don’t remember where they met. They were having events, carnivals. My dad grew up in Cherry Tree [Adair County, Oklahoma]. And my mom, Bunch—that’s where they found each other. That’s all she said. She didn’t tell me anything else.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You don’t need to know.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: “You don’t need to know,” she said. “I’m gonna go get a switch.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I remember, a long time ago they called a carnival a ‘picnic’. They never said ‘carnival’, they said ‘picnic’.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: The people weren’t even mean—just the drunks. The drunks.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes the drunks were funny. A long time ago there were old ladies, where were they? Just around there... and her name was Sali, ᏌᎵ, and [the other was] U⁠na⁠gi⁠ni⁠, ᎤᎾᎩᏂ. At that time the courthouse -- [phone rings] -- at that time the courthouse lawn looked different. On Saturday night we would all be over there, watching the drunks coming out. When one [lady] would come out, they would fight. And then at midnight, they would both go home.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That’s how we passed the time then—watching drunks.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What—you two—what do you do, when you get time to do something? So, what do you do?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I just haul people around. “Take me here, take me there.”

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: And me, anywhere they’re eating, I make bread.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, fry bread.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, fry bread. And I do what I can do to help. I like to do that. And, now because of this (arthritis), they don’t hardly call me. But I still go.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: You need to tell them, “I’ve done my part, I’m tired.”

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I’d still like to do that. But they don’t call me like they used to. It’s because of this, I can’t do it. It’s just my knee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you miss it?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, I do, I do. When I hear that they’re doing something, I just go. I go there.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Sometimes funerals, and dinners.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I like to help those in the church. Where they’re cooking—that’s where I like to be.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you, Oleta?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: And just running around all the time. And Saturday, Sarah told me to take her to Grove. Her hand swelled up, I told her, “We better go to the ER.”

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: What happened?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: That’s just what I did, take them places. When I get time, I visit someone, you know. And pray for them, if they need prayers.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Good, good.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: And, these days, people come to my house for prayers. I used to go to theirs.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: At my house, the phone is always ringing. Like, what just happened happens all the time. They say this is what is happening to us. Then sometimes they’ll be asking, what is the name of the preacher, or a number. Sometimes I would say, “I’m a preacher and I’m sitting right here.” They’d be looking for a different one. And, then if they can’t find one then they would say, “Can you come over?” I would tell them, “Yeah, I guess I can come.” I told my wife, “Boy, I’m a secondhand preacher,” I told her. “When they can’t find anyone, they’ll pick me.” That’s what me and Stanley Grass used to say to each other.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That’s what they know.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They know they can depend on you. That’s why they did that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what they do. And, sometimes late at night, someone will be calling you. Just when you’re snoring really good, someone will call. But also, that is the reason why.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Then you get up.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That’s what we’re here for.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: To help people.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Back then, when you were growing up, when they used to do things—they don’t do that anymore, nowadays. Nowadays, as far as you know. For instance... for instance, ’long time ago, like y’all were saying—if there was an event, the community would help each other. Or if someone passed away, they would visit each other.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They would go there all night. Nowadays, they don’t do that. They will just go for a little while.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: When they would hear about it, they would quickly go and help.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Or they cut wood, if it was winter.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nowadays, they don’t do that.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: No, you have to buy everything now. And, if someone does something for you, you have to pay them. They won’t do it for free. Everything is different nowadays.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Very much so.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: People are very different nowadays.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We think very different, nowadays.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Oh yeah, really.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: The world is changing... it’s not the world, it’s the people. The people have changed completely.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: The world is still here, like it was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what is ruining us.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: It really is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: America’s... even our leaders are doing ugly things.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Nobody is doing the right thing, now.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: The leaders are liars, nowadays. All of them.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: When they say ‘moral values’—that’s what they used to raise us. Don’t be over there lying. If you can’t do anything for anybody, after you have already given your word. So, go back over there, and let them know you’re not going to come and help them out. Tell each other. And nowadays, these children don’t know anything like that.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: They really don’t.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: “Say ‘thank you,’ if someone does something for you,” they used to tell us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Me too, that’s what they told us.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: They used to tell us to help out the elders.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: And we also knew who we were related [to], and nowadays they don’t know. And they would tell us, “That’s your aunt, that’s your uncle. Don’t be going with them, [romantically], they’re related to you.”

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They used to say that.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They would say that, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would always say that to me.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I always heard that, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Even if you were just talking to them. They would say that-One was related to you.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, they would say that. “Don’t be talkin’ to them that much,” they would say. And you couldn’t fight back, back then. I would just say, “OK.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you two’s parents, and our parents? Did they ever tell you about the Trail of Tears? Like, the things that happened, or how they came through?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: And for us, my grandma told me about them coming through. There was a road in Maysville. The people were really crying as they were coming through.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: It was painful coming through.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: It was painful as they were traveling. It was ’long ways.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That’s what she was telling us—my grandma.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it was really painful coming through.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, definitely.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And, now we’ve got it made. They came through very painfully.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: And, we still don’t get it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We don’t think about it.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: We don’t think about it.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: We take advantage of the good stuff, these days, and we don’t care. We don’t do what we’re supposed to do.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And, for me. It’s like we go through a lot of pain raising our grandkids and teaching them things as they’re growing up—so good things can happen. They can find good things to happen to them. It’s kind of the same thing—they went through a painful time. And as for me, it wasn’t that painful.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: We don’t know what’s painful these days. We think so but…

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: It’s nothing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And also, they went through starvation. These days, I don’t see anybody going through starvation.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: It’s their own fault, if they’re starving.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If they’re Cherokees, there’s a place for them to get food.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, really. They feed them everywhere.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I know, really. God treats us really good.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, God really cares for us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, even the non-believers are treated good. Without them realizing it.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Until He gives up on them.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: When God gets tired, He’s going to end it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A while ago I was talking to one of the pastors. They have food for the leader to eat and use that came from North Carolina at the time that they were coming through. They used it for the Lord’s Supper, and they brought it here. I asked him if they could draw it. “Even if you could send it to me through your phone,” I told him. He said, “We have it.” But they really thought a lot of it.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: It’s really precious.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah…

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I would like to see what it looks like.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: How they used it back then, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your parents, you two’s parents, did they make a garden?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: They really did.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They worked really hard, didn’t they?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: And they would put us to work, too, pulling weeds.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: And clearing the poke.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: You couldn’t quit, until you finished. And then you could play, they said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My mom, when she would start a garden, she would say, “Go borrow a hoe.” I would think “Ha!” It would just be one wheel.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, in the front.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You had to push it. And we’d push it around again. And, then it would take us a long time. It was a little bit, about the size of this [gestures] room—it was a little bit bigger. And then, when we would finish, Mom would be right behind me. She was doing this [gestures] with the hoe, fixing it. When we would finish that, we would start planting the garden. Different things. And the tamali... how did you say ‘tomatoes’ a while ago?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: U-nu-gu-hi-s-di.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: U-nu-gu-hi-s-di, yeah. That’s what they call them in North Carolina. U-nu-gu-hi-s-di.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That, and also beans, onion, and potatoes, we would plant.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Lettuce, and different things.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: And potatoes, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [unintelligible] when there would be a lot of it, it would be hot in the kitchen, when water was --

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: -- boiling.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And she would put it in a Mason jar—you two know what that is. She would can it, and then she would put it up. For instance, for Christmas and Thanksgiving, she would take it down.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I remember, when my grandpa was living with us. When they would kill pigs, he would cook all of it and he would put them in jars. It would be like you just killed it a while ago. When he would bring them, in the wintertime. That’s how he did it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about when they used to cook... the intestines?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They were really good, but they stunk when you cooked them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When they were cooked.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: If they’re cleaned good.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Do you like that kind?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Intestines? Yeah, I like them.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Me, too.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I like them, too. We would take them to the creek—Mom and Grandma—we would clean them all really good down there. It was good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It stunk when they would cook them.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That’s why I didn’t like them. That’s what my grandma used to do.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They would eat everything. They didn’t hardly throw anything away.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And, also, head cheese [brawn, meat terrine, jellied meatloaf].

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They would make head cheese, again, back then. I never watched them make it, I didn’t learn.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Me, neither.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Then, again, pigs’ feet.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I really like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Some people didn’t like them, but I would really eat them.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, they’re really good. Same for neckbones.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time, no... late ‘Grandma’... as I was saying, she used to tell me to call her ‘Grandma’. There was a guy that fixed pigs, that lived close by [to Grandma]. He would always send me the ears, because he knew I liked them.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They were good, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, they were good.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: When my dad would kill a hog, we would be waiting to get that white stuff from the head. What’s it called?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, what’s the name of it?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: The brain.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, that was really good. We would all fight over it.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: One person was talking about when they killed a pig, and, when they were cooking. And, some White person came, and they had everything on the table. At the end of the table they had pigs’ --

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: -- feet.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: -- Their feet. A Cherokee said, “Give some of that pigs’ step.” They gave it to him.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Pigs’ step. He didn’t know what to say. They all understood each other even though they misspoke in English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Me and my wife misspeak sometimes.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Mom told us the three-of-Them-that-were-related didn’t go to school one time. They said, “Let’s go the creek and fish.” And their mom thought they were at school, because they used to walk back then [after the school day]. The next morning, the teacher said, “Where were you all yesterday?” and “We just all looked at each other. We didn’t know what to say.” After a while that-Boy said, “Oh we went hooking,” he said. He was trying to say ‘fishing’. “Oh fishing,” she told him, he said.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: They said he told them ‘hooking’.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And, what we were talking about—gardening. Things to... they were looking for in the woods—blueberries and blackberries.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Mushrooms.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Mushrooms.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Wild onions.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wild onions. If you eat that stuff, your bodies will be healthy. Did they tell you all that stuff, and teach y’all good things? Eat good things that don’t hurt your body?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yeah, they taught us that. And, also, the watercress, amayi udu they called it.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: And that was good, too.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I’ve ate everything.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: But that’s all we had, right? We didn’t run to the store every five minutes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I like watercress with grease.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Hot grease, bacon grease.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: With salt.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Hot water cornbread.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nobody will eat it anymore. I don’t even know if it’s around anymore.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Kids, they won’t eat it. They’ll just say, “Ew!”

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I make cornbread like that, sometimes. When I’m really hungry, I’ll make cornbread again. That’s what I put on it—salt. That’s all I put on it, salt. Gaw, it’s good.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Fried.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Grease. When it’s just me and my wife, she’ll make water gravy. And fry bread. She just makes it on top of the pan.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Lazy man bread.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s good to eat.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Sara—‘crazy man bread’. “Make me some crazy man bread,” she said to me. “What?” I told her. That’s what I’m saying, I don’t know if I’m telling you the truth.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What is wrote down here. What do you two think—when you see something wrote in Cherokee—what do y’all think about? What do you feel, when you see something wrote in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I think about church—when they taught Cherokee.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: When I see it somewhere, I try to talk it, ’cause I can. I can talk all of Cherokee. And I just think about that—how proud I am that I can talk it. I mean—that I can read it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And, also, what we were talking about—because us Cherokees, we think different than White people.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Really quick, we can think two ways—the Cherokee, and the English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I had a lot of trouble talking English when I first started school. You would think the White way and the Cherokee way. The White people say, “Why does that happen?” That’s what happens to me, because I’m Cherokee. I told them, “I gotta think White, and I gotta think Cherokee,” I told them.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: We talk two different ways.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One would be funny, and the other wouldn’t.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s not funny, right?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: If you tell it Cherokee, it’s funny, right? If I translated into English, it’s not funny. They would be saying, “What’s so funny?” I tell them, “You don’t understand.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There—some people, in Kenwood, a man and a woman—they were married, but they’re not alive now. The husband was teasing. I don’t remember what they started talking about. “My wife is always chasing me.” She was always chasing him. They were chasing each other. “And you were always chasing me.” “Yeah, really, but you always kept coming back.” That’s what I’m saying, it was two different things.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: It was two different things.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what we’re saying—the Cherokee language can mean two different things. We need to watch what we’re saying, when we’re talking. When we’re talking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Then you might say something different. And, too, when you’re teaching, when you’re teaching. The non-speakers understand. The non-speakers.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: One walked by. He told how I saw him, I think he was in grade school, and they were playing on the playground. There were some White boys that were gathered around. They were amazing about something they were dragging on the ground. They White boys said, “Hey, come here.” And the Cherokee boy came there. “What’s that?” he said. And he was really a... What do you call... a scorpion.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Tsi⁠s⁠dv⁠na⁠, ᏥᏍᏛᎾ. Yeah, tsi⁠s⁠dv⁠na⁠ ᏥᏍᏛᎾ, iyu⁠s⁠di⁠, ᎢᏳᏍᏗ.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: It was funny when he told it: “What’s that?” and the Cherokee speaker said, “My daddy said that’s ‘almost crawdad,’” he said.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: That what the meaning of tsi⁠s⁠dv⁠na⁠ ᏥᏍᏛᎾ, and iyu⁠s⁠di⁠, ᎢᏳᏍᏗ.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: He said it’s ‘almost crawdad’.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: He just translated it, huh? What he knew. That same as when he said, “We went hooking.” It came back around.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about, did they ever tell you two, when they came through, and the things they saw? Some talk about the ‘little people’. Ghosts, and interesting things that they seen. Did they tell you anything about that, when your parents were talking to you? Or, when they were talking, did you hear, what them talking about things?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I’ve heard them saying that. It started from my dad and grandpa. My grandpa was talking about seeing ghosts and stuff like that. That’s where my mom and dad were getting it from—that’s how they knew all that stuff.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They learned to believe. My grandpa used to talk about the ‘little people’.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, them, too.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: If you’re still, you can hear them talking. “They have a road ‘out back’,” he would say—where we lived. I never did hear it. But that’s what he would say [her grandpa]. They would go into the bluff, and they would have snakes for chairs. Snakes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I’ve heard that, too, before.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: That’s what he used to say.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: We would be sitting on the porch, and Grandma would be telling a lot of stories like that. Things that happened, and things that they seen. I felt good when we did that.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: The things they were being told, and they followed what they were being taught.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s where we learned. Sometimes when we’re all at the house, that’s what we like to do. Just talking about things.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: That’s how it used to be a long time ago. There was no TV. They would gather outside and talk. But they would tell us kids, “Go play over there somewhere. Don’t be listening to the adults talking,” they used to tell us. This days, a little kid would know more.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Kids.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: It would know everything.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: These days.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about, did you know, a long time ago, toward-Noche, Stick Spring, there was an old lady?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Ga⁠da⁠tlv⁠, ᎦᏓᏢ.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: And that-One, when we would get together, they would talk about her [Ga⁠da⁠tlv⁠, ᎦᏓᏢ].

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Was she a witch?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, she was a real witch, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what they used to say. One time there was some White people living there, and Curtis Goss lived there. Did you know him? He was always in town, on Main Street sitting around, that Curtis Goss. He left. He took off to Stick Spring. He seen that old lady behind him.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: His church was close to where that woman lived.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It really scared him, and he got. Got out and ran to the house. And through the door and broke it, when he went in. And he told his dad. “It’s alright,” he said. “That’s the old lady living next to you,” he said.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: He already knew.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He already knew.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I guess, a long time ago, there were people like that, ain’t it? A⁠n⁠a⁠t⁠s⁠e⁠l⁠v⁠s⁠g⁠i⁠, ᎠᎾᏤᎸᏍᎩ—in English they call them ‘shape-shifters’.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: When she would come over, she wouldn’t leave till about dark, when Mom is visiting me.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: She wasn’t scared?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: No. And my dad would say, would say “Are you going to have a safe flight, and when you get there, don’t be saying that. Or she’s going to do something to you”

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: She’s going to bother you.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I think she really was a witch. They said she would kill people, if she could—to live longer. That’s what they used to say, killing. I mean that’s all I knew about her.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They would eat the liver, they used to say. I would say, “How would they eat the livers?”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A long time ago there used to be a lady named Ga⁠no⁠lv⁠s⁠ga⁠, ᎦᏃᎸᏍᎦ.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, they were together.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. Her son... there was a hospital a long time ago. They looked at her [Ga⁠no⁠lv⁠s⁠ga⁠, ᎦᏃᎸᏍᎦ], and the doctor was dismissive while he was examining, he said. While he was checking her heart, and looking close to her back --

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: -- listening.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He said, “Hey, [unintelligible],” he called the boy by his name. “This lady sitting here.” “Yeah?” “She don’t even have a drop a blood in her,” he said. The doctor said, and boy was shaking his head.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Wonder what it was?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was a witch.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Oh, it was a witch.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I think her name was Ga⁠no⁠lv⁠s⁠ga⁠, ᎦᏃᎸᏍᎦ. I think.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, they were together. And, that-One, the late Ga⁠lo⁠nv⁠ni⁠, ᎦᎶᏅᏂ. He’s back was blue, they said. He was in pain. “While we were looking for huckleberries, I fell,” he said. They said someone hit him.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: A ‘shape-shifter’.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: They said it was a pig. Someone hit it.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: He shape-shifted into a pig. That’s what they used to do—make themself into something. I guess that’s why they call them shape-shifters.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That’s what she said they had said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it was really like that.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: When she passed... no she didn’t pass. When she was really sick, she was calling on my sister. She wanted to talk with her. So, I went with her [my sister]. Just to be nosey. There to her house—birds... not birds—owls, all over, they were crawling all over.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Underneath or outside?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: On top of the house, on the roof. And they were yelling. She was really a shape-shifting, Da⁠do⁠tlv⁠ni⁠, ᏓᏙᏢᏂ.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I guess she had those to watch her.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: It was real, that was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, she was real.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: My daughter. My... my daughter... my sister—we would sew at her house. You know how they would hang the quilts? You know that kind?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: They would hang them.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: They’d put it down. And Ella, you know Ella? That-one was a baby at that time. She put a quilt underneath, when they would sew. She laid the baby down there. Then that-one got choked on something. “And I cleaned everything good before I laid it down,” she said. U⁠do⁠tlv⁠nv⁠, ᎤᏙᏢᏅ, threw something down and I guess she picked it up and ate it. I mean she tried to put it in her mouth.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: That was a mean old lady.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That’s what they say. So... I got a picture of her.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: But she was really nice.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She was nice. Sometimes. Chester Jones, did you know him? Noche—that’s where that old lady went to church.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, she did.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When she would tell us to take her back. “Will y’all take me back?” We would take her back. “Wait for a little while. I am going to show you all appreciation.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There was just a little building, kind of like a well-house. There was a sound coming from there. Say like a dish-pan–that-they-used-to-have, a long time ago, when they used to clean them, a long time ago—that was the same sound it was making. Someone would come and give her money. That is how much money she had, is what they used to say.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: She must have found it while she was shape-shifting.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Chester Jones was saying, “It’s enough, it’s enough.” She was saying, “No, no, take it. You all take it.” We were afraid so we took it.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: There’s this one thing that I know, have experienced. One time we dismissed church at Round Springs. Archie Sharp, do you remember him? One time he said, “Let’s stop by there,” ...How he related to him? ...It was Frank Arneecher’s mother. “Let’s stop by there and have a prayer service.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: We got there. That-one’s bed was just this tall [gestures]. That-one was laying there, when we went in there. That-one probably didn’t know we were going to be there. So, we went in. What’s that-one’s name in Cherokee? That-one had a name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was that-one’s name?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: So, he [Archie] asked that-one, “What’s going on, are you sick?” “No, I wasn’t sick. I just fell off the bed,” he said. It was wet everywhere. Yeah, her dress. She was wearing a dress. It was all wet. They asked her what happened, and she said, “I just fell from here.” And the bed she was laying on was just this tall [gestures].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was her name? I forget what her name was.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: She was kind of scary.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: What was her name, in English?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I don’t know... that was Frank Arneecher’s mother.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That was Arneecher... I know the name, but I forgot.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I forget what his name is, too.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: He was talking about the last time... [unintelligible] He said he took a picture of us, standing in front of the closet. She said all you could see, when the picture came back, was her face. All you could see was her face—just her face.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I forget what that name was.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Me too, I forget.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Me too, I forget.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I forget, too. Because of that guy she was married to last—didn’t she have a man towards-the-last?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: I don’t know. She was already old, back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She had already passed away.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: She probably was, yeah. She had wet clothes on, just... she had drowned or jumped in the water. They asked her, “What happened?” She said, “I fell from here.” There was no water there. He told her, “Oh OK.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess they had been swimming.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: She either been swimming, or dove in the water.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Or, she was flying?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Did you drown while you were flying around?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Somebody was telling us. One time, Udotlvni, and Gulonvsgi, and some other old lady—they caught them swimming. One time in the evening. They said they were cleaning up, or doing something. Those three old ladies were swimming.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Was the other one Gategi? She was little. Her name was Gategi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They... really... some... a long time ago. They would lock the door to that-one’s room... to that-one’s room. Then, after a while, they would be talking to the police. They would be saying, “We have your old lady over here.” That old lady would be walking on the sidewalk. And they would catch her and put her in. And wait for them to come and get her. They would have her locked up.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: She would get out. She was probably crawling under the door.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: I never heard that before, about her.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you remember, the Cherokee singers of ’long time ago—they sang old songs?
Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do y’all know a song they sang in Cherokee, ’long time ago—it sounded beautiful?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: ‘One Drop of Blood’?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yeah, and also, ‘Amazing Grace’ in Cherokee. That is what I like.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Will y’all sing one?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Amazing Grace.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: You lead it.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Go ahead.
[Oleta Pritchett & Wallora Kingfisher sing ‘Amazing Grace’]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Amen. That is beautiful, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Praise God.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That tells ’bout a lot, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Yes, it really does.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Absolutely.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: It tells it all, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: No misunderstanding.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: Our God is really merciful—that is what it is talking about. No matter what we have done, He still will not let us go.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: You can say two things: Amazing Grace.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: His mercy endures forever.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: His mercy is forever—that is true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We are underneath that, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: We are underneath that.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
segments.translation: That is the only reason we are here because of His grace.

segments.speaker: oleta-pritchett
segments.translation: We had a pretty bad tornado that came through Jay, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, we still made it through, it didn’t really hit us good.

segments.speaker: wallora-kingfisher
